slides.title: The whole course is one order's journey
slides.notes: Read the boxes left to right, then right to left along the bottom. T1 asks why sell online at all. T2 asks where to sell (own site vs marketplace). T3 sets the price using data. T4 plans inventory across warehouses. T5 picks the equipment. T6 picks the order inside the warehouse. T7 delivers it. T8 explains platform economics and network effects. T9 joins online and offline back together. Every topic aims at the same three outcomes: revenue up, cost down, service level up. The hidden cost of going online is fulfilment: order picking is about 55% of warehouse operating cost and the last mile can be up to 28% of total delivery cost.

slides.purpose: Why sell online? What do you gain and what new costs appear?
slides.notes: Topic 1 sets up the whole course: online retailing removes stores but creates fulfilment and shipping costs. Source: slides01, textbook Ch 1, Wharton case Online Book Retailing.

slides.title: Going online moves the cost from stores to fulfilment
slides.caption: Online: no stores to run, but every order must be picked and delivered. Fulfilment + shipping cost is THE challenge.
slides.notes: B&M retailers ship in bulk to stores (weekly) and customers do the last mile themselves. Online retailers process orders almost continuously (picked within ~30 min) and pay for picking plus delivery to each customer. Amazon gets 400+ orders per second on Cyber Monday. Amazon's fulfilment plus shipping costs kept rising over time.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: where the cost moves
imgs: B&M ships to stores; online ships to every customer
Amazon's fulfilment + shipping cost keeps climbing
slides.takeaway: Online removes stores but adds picking + delivery for every single order. That cost line only goes up as volume grows.
slides.notes: Slide 6 (left) is the core picture of Topic 1 and returns in Topic 4: the B&M chain ends at stores, while the online chain fans out to every customer. Slide 4 (right) shows Amazon's logistics costs rising from about 15.6% to 32.3% of net sales (2009–2021).

slides.title: 14 advantages of online retailing

t: Less inventory: pooled in a few DCs
Cash cycle: paid 19 days before paying suppliers
Flexible fulfilment: any FC serves any zone

slides.notes: Textbook lists 14: no stores; easier market access; less inventory; attractive cash conversion cycle; easier assortment decision; demand data not just sales data; personalised service; locate in convenient states; flexible fulfilment; easier tracking; less damage; diversify products; diversify beyond a country; sales taxes. Remember the catch on diversification: more back-end investment, lower margins, different inventory turns, different packing equipment, and more inventory.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: cash cycle and flexibility
imgs: Cash conversion cycle: Amazon −19 days vs book retailer +78 days
Flexible fulfilment: any FC can serve any zone
slides.takeaway: Amazon is paid by customers ~19 days BEFORE it pays suppliers; a typical book retailer pays suppliers first and waits 78 days.
slides.notes: Left (slide 9): Amazon's operating cycle in 2007: book enters inventory day 0, customer pays around day 28–31, supplier is paid day 50, so cash comes in 19 days before it goes out. Typical book retailer: supplier paid day 90, customer pays day 168, so a 78-day gap (your class note: B&N pays supplier first). Right (slide 15): warehouses can serve any zone; the arrows are reactive (pull) fulfilment, which links to Topic 4.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: assortment and location
imgs: FCs placed near population density ('convenient' states)
slides.takeaway: One website = one assortment decision; FCs follow population density to cut delivery time and shipping cost.
slides.notes: Your class note on slide 14: the correlation between warehouse locations and population density is a fulfilment KPI. Slide 10 note: the assortment decision is easier and can use algorithms and AI.

slides.title: 5 disadvantages: the price of having no store

t: Supplier links, price updates, tracking, security
Never stops: class answer = VARIABLE cost

slides.notes: Exam trap: online is MORE exposed to seasonal spikes because each order is picked after it arrives (make-to-order). Slide 19 asks: is technology a fixed or a variable cost? Your class note records Prof Lim's answer: VARIABLE. Tech spending never stops: software to link more suppliers, constant price and shipping updates, tracking, and ever-newer security. It grows with the business rather than being a one-off investment.

slides.title: Case: Amazon vs Barnes & Noble vs Borders
head: Amazon
Barnes & Noble / BN.com
Borders
rows: 'Sell all, carry few': 2,000 titles stocked of 1M+ listed (1995); drop-ship rest
793 stores; BN.com a separate company (to avoid sales tax); stocked 600–750k titles
Outsourced its website to Amazon, then went cross-channel (2008)
80% of IT spend on back-office logistics; inventory turns ~14×/yr
BN.com never profitable; taken back 2003; added kiosks + buy-online-pick-up-in-store
slides.takeaway: A strong store brand does not transfer online by itself. Logistics is 'the iceberg below the waterline' (Bezos).
slides.notes: Other case facts: online return rates 1–2% vs 10–15× higher for B&M. Amazon's warehouse expansion caused split shipments, higher inventory from more stocking points and IT coordination costs, so it closed McDonough, Georgia in 2001. Amazon net income fell 47% in 2006 as product variety and free shipping (Prime, $79/yr) grew.

slides.title: In-class Q: should B&N integrate online and offline?

t: Order in store when a title is out of stock (save the sale)
Buy online, pick up in store: no last-mile cost, more foot traffic
Pooled inventory and shared customer data
Systems that cannot see store stock
Different picking: single units vs cartons
Channel conflict: who gets credit for the sale?
Tax/legal structure, staff training, consistent prices

slides.notes: This is the textbook Ch 1 'Problems' question and the slide 21 discussion. Structure any answer as benefits for revenue, cost and service, then the operational barriers.

slides.title: Prof Lim's in-lecture questions (T1), answered

items.q: Amazon carries less inventory, but still some. Why? Why several fulfilment centres?
a: Drop-shipping is too slow and unreliable at scale; own stock gives speed and service control
Pooled safety stock still needs to sit somewhere
Several FCs near customers: faster delivery, lower outbound shipping, more capacity, tax/location benefits

items.q: Why is the cash conversion cycle attractive?
a: High inventory turns ('stock-less' model)
Customers pay by card at once; suppliers paid later
Result: −19 days: customers' cash funds the business

items.q: Is technology a fixed or a variable cost?
a: Class answer: VARIABLE (it never stops)
Keeps growing: link more suppliers, update prices and shipping options, tracking, new security
So it is not a one-off fixed investment

slides.notes: These questions are written into slides 8, 9 and 19 of the Topic 1 deck. The fixed vs variable answer follows your class note on slide 19 ('Tech is variable cost'). If an exam question asks it, give the class answer and the reason: spending keeps rising with suppliers, products, orders and security threats.

Possibly lower-margin products; very different inventory turns

items.q: Diversifying beyond the USA: what problems?
a: More stocking points → more inventory
Complex trade rules and customs
(Benefit: sales-tax advantage when choosing FC locations)

items.q: Why are fulfilment costs high, and hard to cut?
a: Manual labour: picking is ~55% of warehouse cost
Each order shipped to each home; returns
Hard to cut: piece picking is hard to automate; spiky demand; huge variety; customers expect fast, free delivery

slides.purpose: Where to sell? Own website, a marketplace, or a marketplace that also fulfils?
slides.notes: Source: slides02, textbook Ch 2, Lim, Wang & Wu (2015) consignment contracts paper.

slides.title: Two business models: who stores and ships?

t: Sellers more independent; easy to leave
Seller sends stock to Amazon FIRST

slides.notes: Other examples: Sell on Lazada vs Sell on Lazada with delivery; VIP.com. Under FBA Amazon charges only when a unit sells, keeps a percentage and returns unsold units after a period.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: the three flows in each model
imgs: Sell on Amazon: seller ships (marketplace never sees the product)
Fulfilment by Amazon: seller ships stock to Amazon first; Amazon delivers
slides.takeaway: Follow the arrows: information (dashed), material (red), money (dotted). In FBA the MATERIAL flow passes through the marketplace too.
slides.notes: Your class notes: in SoA the marketplace earns by taking a cut of the selling price, and setting the commission is complicated. In FBA the contract typically lasts about 6 months, and the seller still owns the inventory (similar to consignment). Prof Lim: 'The most powerful thing to learn is the business model.'

slides.title: Why does a retailer run a marketplace at all?

t: Offer everything without owning all the stock
Outsource the LONG TAIL: slow movers & new items

slides.notes: Long-tail effect: a few products account for most sales, many products have very low demand. A marketplace lets the retailer cover the tail with other people's inventory.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slide: the long tail
points: Red = few best sellers (retailer stocks these itself)
Yellow = long tail of slow movers: let third-party sellers carry them
Result: one-stop shop WITHOUT owning all inventory
Also: test new products; use marketplace data
slides.notes: Your class note: the horizontal axis is products/SKUs. The retailer outsources the long-tail products and expands its product scope. An SKU (stock keeping unit) is a unique code for one product variant.

slides.title: Selling on a marketplace: the seller's view

t: Risk control: unpaid bills, fraud, disputes

slides.notes: Amazon fees are commission-based; Taobao/Tmall charge for advertising. Sellers on their own website have full control and higher margins but must pay to build traffic.

slides.title: Why the operator prefers FBA + consignment

t: Protects brand by controlling service quality
Sellers find it harder to leave (lock-in)
No need to negotiate price/quantity per seller

slides.notes: Consignment: the manufacturer owns the stock until it sells. For each unit sold, the retailer keeps r × price and the manufacturer gets (1 − r) × price.

slides.title: Prof Lim's model: a Stackelberg game (solve backwards)

rows.label: Moves
steps: Retailer (LEADER) sets revenue share r + storage fee s
Each manufacturer (FOLLOWER) picks price p and quantity q

slides.caption: Results: similar manufacturing costs → s = 0 is enough · very different costs → s > 0 (diamond vs diaper) · bigger capacity V can help BOTH sides
slides.notes: Set-up: single period; random price-sensitive demand D = a p^(−b) ε; manufacturer cost M = m + s v; retailer cost R = d − s v. Retailer maximises expected profit knowing the manufacturers' best responses. Storage fee charges bulky cheap goods (diapers) so space is left for valuable small goods (diamonds).

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: the model set-up
imgs: Retailer sets common revenue share r; capacity Σqᵢvᵢ ≤ V
Consignment: maker owns stock until sold; r·p to retailer (e.g. r = 15%)
slides.takeaway: Single period ≈ one ~6-month Amazon contract. Amazon uses r (and s) to control how much each seller ships in.
slides.notes: Your class notes: R = revenue share (e.g. 10–15%), D = demand, p = price, q = quantity, v = volume. Amazon needs to control r to limit sellers' quantities because warehouse space is limited. Different product categories (books, cosmetics) may have different r in practice.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: the two answers from game theory
imgs: Diapers vs diamonds: charge storage fee s > 0 when costs differ a lot
Expanding capacity V raises BOTH retailer and maker profits
slides.takeaway: s = 0 if manufacturing costs are similar; s > 0 if very different (bulky, cheap items pay for space). Bigger V = win-win, with a saturation point.
slides.notes: Handwritten notes on the slides: Amazon charges storage to deter sellers of bulky, low-value items and prefers diamonds (small space, high profit). With more space Amazon can serve more sellers, but there is a saturation point where customers will not buy more.

slides.title: Discussion: SoA or FBA? Who is it better for?

t: Scale economies in its own warehouses
FBA: Prime badge, less work, pro logistics, shipping discounts
But: storage fees, lose customer data, lock-in
SoA suits bulky, slow, custom or high-margin goods
FBA suits small, fast-moving, standard goods

slides.notes: Textbook Ch 2 Problems 1 and 2. A good answer always says 'it depends on the product and the seller's own logistics capability'.

slides.title: T2 exam traps & 'if asked X, say Y'
traps: In the game the RETAILER moves first (leader)
Storage fee s is per unit of VOLUME
'Expanding capacity hurts sellers' ✗: it can help both
Pure-play marketplaces (Taobao, eBay) own no stock
asks: When should s > 0?
When products' manufacturing costs differ a lot
3 reasons to run a marketplace?
One-stop shop (long tail), test products, use data
Why consignment?
No overstock risk, no negotiation, easy split online
slides.notes: Types table: B2B retailer Office Depot; B2B marketplace Alibaba; B2C retailer JD; B2C marketplace Lazada; C2C eBay, Taobao. Service marketplaces: Foodpanda, Airbnb, Uber/Grab, Mechanical Turk.

slides.title: T2 in 60 seconds
points: Marketplace = sell others' goods without owning them
SoA: seller ships · FBA: Amazon ships (operator prefers)
Seller: 5 pros (traffic, trust…) vs 5 cons (fees, rules…)

s = 0 if costs similar; bigger V can help everyone

slides.purpose: What price? Use data to predict demand, then optimise price within business rules.
slides.notes: Source: slides03, textbook Ch 3, HBS case Flashion: Art vs Science in Fashion Retailing (with data file).

slides.title: Online flash sales: why pricing is hard
slides.notes: Assortment changes weekly or even several times a day, while traditional retailers change only a few times a year. Price is fixed during an event. Leftover stock goes into a later event.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: how flash sales run, and the pricing clue
imgs: Procurement → event planning → event sales → leftover goes to a later event
First-exposure sell-through: prices too high? too low?
slides.takeaway: ~50% of first-exposure styles SELL OUT (price may be too LOW); ~15% sell < 25% (price too HIGH). Both are lost money.
slides.notes: In-lecture question on slide 15: are prices too high or too low? Answer: both. The tall bar at 'sold out' suggests many prices were too low (you could raise price and still sell through). The bars on the left (0–25% sold) suggest prices too high. So the challenge is to predict demand and optimise price for each first-exposure style.

slides.title: Art or science? Can data price fashion?

t: Hard to measure colour, style, quality
Value differs from person to person
One wrong prediction has small impact

slides.notes: Prof Lim's conclusion: the approach is scientific but not free of art. Choosing the features (X1, X2, …) and spotting derived and missing data is art.

slides.title: From data to price in 3 steps

rows.label: Method
steps: 2 · Predict demand: Y = a + bX (regression / ML)
3 · Optimise price: max X·Y subject to constraints

slides.caption: Data: AVAILABLE price, MSRP, timing, competitor price, sales · DERIVED discount, # styles, relative price, weekend · MISSING lost sales
slides.notes: Lost sales are missing because when a style sells out you never see the extra customers who wanted it (censored demand). Pricing considerations: demand, competitor prices, trends, assortment, inventory, target margin, target sell-through, macro factors, own stock vs drop-ship, promotions, discount price points (e.g., minimum $9).

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: fitting the demand line
imgs: Use past data of similar styles to find a and b
slides.takeaway: Regression finds a = 70.51 and b = −0.607: each extra $1 loses ~0.6 customers. Price explains ~84% of demand variation.
slides.notes: Your notes: R² of about 0.84 means price alone explains 84% of the variation, and the price coefficient is highly significant. In practice (the real Rue La La study by Ferreira et al. 2016), regression trees and random forests beat linear regression and lifted revenue about 10%, but the class uses linear regression to show the logic.

slides.title: Worked example: the margin floor decides the price
slides.notes: Demand from regression: Y = 70.50719 − 0.60658X. Unit cost 75. Constraints: X ≤ 134.99 (competitor), (X − 75)/75 ≥ 0.5 so X ≥ 112.5, and X ≥ 5. Revenue X·Y peaks at X = 70.50719 / (2 × 0.60658) = 58.12, which is NOT allowed. Revenue falls after 58.12, so the best allowed price is the lowest allowed price: X* = 112.5 (revenue about 255). The margin constraint binds; the competitor cap does not.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slide: the constraints that set the price
points: Objective: max X(70.50719 − 0.60658X)
X ≤ 134.99 (competitor's price)
(X − 75)/75 ≥ 0.5 → X ≥ 112.5 (50% margin on unit cost 75)
X ≥ 5 (discount price point)
MATLAB answer: optimal price = 112.50
slides.notes: Slide 30 labels each constraint. Revenue peaks at X ≈ 58 (below the $75 unit cost, so you would lose money on every unit). The margin rule is binding, so the solver sits exactly on 112.50.

slides.title: AI: two approaches, and why data is the new oil

t: Layers of artificial neurons learn from labelled examples
Needs lots of DATA + computing power
Uses: faces, speech, translation, fraud, driving
Average engineers + lots of data beat experts + little data

slides.takeaway: 'If AI is the electricity, data is the oil.'
slides.notes: Discussion question in class: which AI technology will have the biggest impact in the next 10–20 years and why? Good answers link to data availability and operations (e.g., autonomous vehicles in last mile, demand forecasting, robotics).

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: neural networks learn from labelled data
imgs: Layers of artificial neurons copy the brain's structure
Feed many 'panda' / 'no panda' images; the program finds the features
slides.takeaway: Rule-based = humans write the rules. Neural nets = the computer learns the rules from data. More data → smarter AI.
slides.notes: Slides 36–42. The panda example: rule-based says 'round + black-and-white patches = panda' and fails on complex images; neural networks learn from thousands of labelled images.

slides.title: Discussion: which AI will matter most by 2045?

items.q: A strong answer: language models + 'agentic' AI
a: Breadth: language is the interface to most work (law, health, education, code, service)
Lowers barriers: buyers could ask an AI for a price (Flashion's trust problem)
Data-hungry and improves with data + compute: 'data is the oil'

items.q: Strong alternatives to mention
a: AI in healthcare/biology (drug design, diagnosis)
Autonomous vehicles and robots (links to T6 robots, T7 last mile)
Recommendation algorithms (shape what billions buy and see)

items.q: How to structure it in the exam
a: Pick ONE and say why: scale × data × how many people it touches
Use a course example
Note one risk (jobs, bias, privacy) and one alternative

slides.notes: Slide 32. There is no single right answer; marks come from a clear choice, a reason linked to data and computing power (slides 39–43), a course example and a fair alternative.

slides.title: Case: Flashion: Art vs Science (HBS)

t: Kate Wilson (data scientist) vs Priscilla Johnson ('pricing is an art')
~5M members; 24-hour events; ~50% of sales in hour 1
Buyers target 80% sell-through; no markdowns mid-event
Data: 30,389 styles; avg sell-through 69%; 46% sold out
Combine: the model forecasts and suggests a price
The buyer adds judgement and signs off
Optimise revenue/profit, not just the 80% target
Win sceptics with a pilot or A/B test

slides.notes: Data file regression (own calculation): sell-through ≈ 0.32 + 0.97 × discount. Discount = (MSRP − price)/MSRP. Sold-out styles hide true demand (censored). Drop-shipping means Flashion does not own the stock.

slides.title: Flashion's data file: what the numbers say
body: Deeper discount → higher sell-through: ≤20% off sells ~41%; >60% off sells ~92% (sell-through ≈ 0.32 + 0.97 × discount)
Weekend events sell slightly less; sold-out styles HIDE true demand (censored), so the model under-counts best sellers
slides.notes: Own analysis of the case Excel file (sheet 'data': 30,389 rows, 1,000 events, Oct–Dec). Formulas: discount = (MSRP − price)/MSRP; sell-through = units sold / starting inventory. Average price $282, cost $216, MSRP $425. The case text says 'over half' sell out because Exhibit 2 shows only some departments; the full data gives 46%. Use these to show you understand why 'science' needs good data, and why lost sales are the missing piece.

slides.title: T3 exam traps & 'if asked X, say Y'
traps: Regression finds a and b; OPTIMISATION finds the price X
Unconstrained best price (58.12) ≠ constrained optimum (112.5)
Lost sales are MISSING data, not derived
Lecture margin is on COST: (X − 75)/75 ≥ 50%
asks: Is pricing art or science?
Mostly science, but feature choice is art; combine model + buyer
Why more data beats smarter experts?
Neural nets learn patterns from data; accuracy grows with data
Which constraint binds in the example?
The 50% margin floor (X ≥ 112.5)
slides.notes: Write the price formula on your A4 sheet: X⁰ = −a/(2b), then check constraints.

slides.title: T3 in 60 seconds
points: Flash sales: first-exposure styles are the pricing problem
Art vs science → combine both
Data → regression Y = a + bX → max X·Y with constraints
Example answer X* = 112.5 (margin floor binds)

slides.purpose: Plan the supply chain: what to order, where to store it, which warehouse ships it.
slides.notes: Source: slides04, textbook Ch 4, Lim, Jiu & Ang (2021) robust optimisation paper; Forbes article on Amazon and Alibaba.

slides.title: Offline vs online fulfilment are different jobs

t: NO fulfilment flexibility: if one warehouse is out, no retrieval from another
FULFILMENT FLEXIBILITY: any warehouse holding stock can serve the zone

slides.takeaway: '兵马未动，粮草先行': supplies move before the troops. SCM is a core competency.
slides.notes: Cao Cao beat Yuan Shao in the Three Kingdoms by attacking his supplies. Fulfilment flexibility raises service levels but can raise outbound shipping cost and makes allocation and replenishment harder.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: online demand and flexibility
imgs: Offline: few, large orders to stores · Online: many, small orders to homes
If one warehouse is out of stock, another can serve the zone
slides.takeaway: Fulfilment flexibility is the online advantage, but it couples the three planning decisions together.
slides.notes: Slide 12 lists the four differences. Slide 14 shows the red 'out of stock' warehouse and red arrows from other warehouses: this is fulfilment flexibility.

slides.title: The 3 decisions of aggregate supply chain planning

rows.label: Decisions
steps: ① REPLENISH: when & how much to order
② ALLOCATE: how much in each warehouse

slides.caption: PUSH (anticipative, before demand is known) = ① + ②   ·   PULL (reactive, after demand is known) = ③
slides.notes: Replenishment trades off fixed ordering cost against holding cost. Allocation keeps each product's stock close to its demand. Fulfilment picks the warehouse that minimises shipping cost once demand is known. Because of fulfilment flexibility, all three must be decided JOINTLY.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: push before demand, pull after demand
imgs: Push (anticipative) up to the warehouses; pull (reactive) after
The model: push-pull boundary sits at the warehouses
slides.takeaway: Replenish + allocate = PUSH (before demand is known). Fulfil = PULL (after demand is realised).
slides.notes: The dotted push-pull boundary at the warehouses is the key image for this topic.

slides.title: JRAF: joint replenishment-allocation-fulfilment model

t: Supplier capacity · everything received is allocated
Flow balance; drop-ship = 'FC J+1' keeps it feasible

slides.notes: Decision variables: x (replenishment), v (allocation), w (fulfilment), y (inventory). Drop-shipping is expensive but always available, so the model always has a feasible solution. Solve with off-the-shelf software; the robust version handles uncertain demand.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: the JRAF model
imgs: x = replenish, v = allocate, w = fulfil, y = inventory; J+1 = drop-ship
Objective: production + holding + allocation + fulfilment costs
slides.takeaway: You do not need to solve it; know the 3 decision types, 4 cost terms, 5 constraint types and why drop-shipping (J+1) keeps it feasible.
slides.notes: Your class notes: FC = fulfilment centre; t = 1, 2, … are periods (e.g. Monday, Tuesday); x = how much to order from each supplier; v = how much to allocate to each FC; w = how much to ship from FC j to zone k; y = inventory level; δ = yes/no order switch (fixed setup cost only if you order); J+1 = drop-shipping channel. Constraints: supplier capacity; all received stock allocated; warehouse capacity (current stock + new arrivals ≤ capacity); demand fully met; flow balance (next stock = current + allocated − shipped). Solved with off-the-shelf software (Lim, Jiu & Ang 2021).

slides.title: Reading: Amazon & Alibaba bet the future on SCM
stats: parcels Amazon shipped of its own goods in a year
Amazon doubled its leased cargo-jet fleet
body: Lesson: logistics becomes the critical success factor, so retailers integrate vertically
Amazon was forecast to out-ship FedEx by 2019; drones target 30-minute delivery
slides.notes: Forbes, May 2016. Walmart's sales were still 4× Amazon's at the time. Cainiao covers 600+ cities in 31 provinces.

traps: Allocation is PUSH (anticipative), not pull

slides.purpose: Choose the kit: match storage and handling equipment to pallet, case or piece demand.
slides.notes: Source: slides05, textbook Ch 5, Group 1 Week 4 submission.

slides.notes: The fast-pick area is a premier region, typically near the shipping department, restocked from reserve. Then two different picking strategies: fast movers (bucket brigades) and slow movers (routing heuristics or robots).

Popular items on gravity flow racks; long tail on bin-shelving
slides.takeaway: A fast-pick area is a 'warehouse within a warehouse': small, near shipping, restocked from reserve. It cuts response time.
slides.notes: Your notes: a bigger fast-pick area holds more SKUs and needs less restocking, while a smaller one cuts travel but needs more restocking. The best design balances pick savings against replenishment work.

slides.title: From fixed zones to bucket brigades
imgs: Zone picking: each worker owns a fixed zone
Work sharing: cross-trained workers help neighbours
Bucket brigade: the last worker walks back…
…takes over the job behind, and so on back to the start
slides.notes: Your notes: zone picking creates WIP in front of the slowest worker and leaves others idle, because a static assignment is used in a changing system. Cross-training adds flexibility, but needs a clear rule to coordinate. The bucket brigade is that rule.

slides.title: Step 2: fast movers: the bucket brigade
slides.notes: Rule: carry your job forward until the colleague downstream takes it over (or you finish at the end of the line). Then walk back and take over the job of your upstream colleague (or start a new job if you are first). Model assumptions: work content 1 spread evenly; constant forward speeds; instant walk-back; no passing. If workers are ordered slowest to fastest, hand-off points converge and the line self-balances. Worker i repeats the interval from (v1+…+v(i−1))/Σv to (v1+…+vi)/Σv, and throughput is the sum of speeds. Example: speeds 1, 2, 3 give intervals [0, 1/6], [1/6, 1/2], [1/2, 1] and TH = 6. Path to bucket brigades: zone picking → cross-training → work sharing → bucket brigades.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: the model and self-balancing
imgs: Assumptions: work = 1, constant speed vᵢ, instant walk-back, no passing
slides.takeaway: In the time–work chart (right), the hand-off points quickly settle at fixed spots: the line balances itself.
slides.notes: Your note on slide 31: the line is balanced because, in the long run, the repetition and efficiency conditions are both met.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: the formula, and the real-world result
imgs: 3 workers: intervals and TH = v₁ + v₂ + v₃
Real case: pick rate jumped after switching to bucket brigades
slides.takeaway: Faster workers get larger shares. Throughput = sum of speeds. A real warehouse saw productivity rise after the switch.
slides.notes: Slide 34 compares zone picking and bucket brigades: zone picking cannot handle task-time detail, balances only on average and cannot adjust to absences; bucket brigades need no work-content model, seek balance job by job, and adapt to disruptions and seasonality.

slides.title: The tipping point: p* = r(z)·f(z) = z(1 − z)
slides.notes: With network effects, consumer x will pay r(x)·f(z) where z is the fraction using the good, f increasing, f(0) = 0. z = 0 is always an equilibrium: if nobody expects anyone to buy, the good is worth 0. Other equilibria solve p* = r(z)f(z). With r(x) = 1 − x and f(z) = z, the curve z(1 − z) peaks at 1/4 when z = 1/2. For 0 < p* < 1/4 there are two solutions z′ < z″. z′ is UNSTABLE (the tipping point / critical mass): below it users leave and demand falls to 0; between z′ and z″ users join and demand rises to z″. z″ is STABLE. Formula: z = [1 ± √(1 − 4p)]/2. p = 0.16 → 0.2 and 0.8. p = 0.09 → 0.1 and 0.9. If p > 1/4 only z = 0 survives.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: without vs with network effects
imgs: No network effect: one equilibrium where r(x) = p
With: r(z)f(z) = z(1 − z) → two crossings z′ and z″
slides.takeaway: Without network effects, one equilibrium. With them, three: 0, z′ and z″.
slides.notes: Handwritten note on slide 32: with positive externalities, the larger z, the larger f(z). Note on slide 31: z = 0 is an equilibrium where no one buys; p* is the retail price.

slides.title: Prof Lim's slides: stability and lower prices

slides.takeaway: z′ is the 'hump the firm must get over'. Lowering price makes the hump smaller AND the final market bigger.

slides.takeaway: Grand integration (6): e-commerce, logistics, B&M retail, cloud, e-payment, AI/autonomous tech (Alibaba, Amazon, JD)
slides.notes: Rigby (HBR 2011): US e-commerce 9% of retail, heading to 15–20%; digital influences about 50% of store sales; Amazon 5-year ROI 17% vs 6.5% for traditional retailers despite a lower margin (4% vs 6%): judge by ROIC and growth, not margin. Stores lift nearby online share (5% vs 3%). Retail is disrupted about every 50 years.

slides.title: Reading: The Future of Shopping (Rigby, HBR 2011)
stats: US retail sales online (2011), heading to 15–20%
of store sales influenced by digital
Tesco Homeplus online sales (QR subway store)
body: Amazon's margin (4%) was LOWER than rivals' (6%), but its return on capital was more than double → judge retailers by ROIC and growth, not margin or same-store sales
Retail is disrupted about every 50 years; stores near online customers lift online sales (5% vs 3%); test and learn, then commit
slides.notes: Rigby's advice: redesign from scratch, map customer pathways, turn stores into experiences (don't cut staff into a death spiral), use tech in store (tablets, virtual mirrors, mobile checkout), test like clinical trials (PetSmart, Boots), keep the digital team separate but coordinated (like a satellite: not too far, not too close).
